prompt: In some countries, cash is being replaced almost entirely by digital payment. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
Almost every figure produced about going cashless is an average, and an average is the wrong instrument here. The convenience is spread thinly across millions of people who barely notice it. The harm is concentrated on a few thousand who lose the ability to buy things. I think the development is positive, but only in the sense that a sound policy can be handled badly, and most countries are handling this one badly.

The case for it is not in doubt. Handling notes is expensive for banks and for shops; stealing cash in quantity has largely stopped being worth the effort; a card can be cancelled in a minute and a wallet cannot. Payments that leave a record are harder to conceal from a tax authority, and the same record gives an ordinary household a picture of its own spending that it never previously had. These are real gains and they accrue to nearly everybody.

The losses accrue to people who can be named. Someone who never acquired a smartphone, or whose last bank branch within reach has closed, does not experience a cashless economy as slightly less convenient. They experience it as being unable to pay for a bus. Nor is this a transitional problem that time will solve, because the group most affected is the group least likely to change. A system can reach ninety-five per cent adoption while the remaining five per cent are simply shut out of ordinary life.

So the answer turns on whether cash is retained as an obligation rather than as a habit. A country that keeps a legal duty to accept it, and guarantees a basic account to anyone who asks, gets the benefits without abandoning anyone. A country that lets cash lapse because most people stopped using it has made a change that is positive on the spreadsheet and quietly punitive at the edges.
title: Cash disappearing in favour of digital payment
